Questions for presentation preparation

1. What does the title ask?

How household-specific job access and earning opportunities change inequality in the declared ex-ante monetary level, separately from preferences, resources and needs.

2. Does income alone reveal constraints?

No. Similar earnings and hours can reflect different tastes, opportunities and family resources.

3. What does RURO mean?

Random Utility–Random Opportunity: observed job choice reflects both utility and a structural opportunity measure.

4. Is joint estimation new here?

No. It is inherited, especially from the applied RURO literature; the contribution is the cross-sectional welfare estimand and attribution.

5. Is the first picture the welfare metric?

No. It motivates preference–opportunity ambiguity; the second picture draws the implemented flat-consumption reference.

6. Which year is the income reference?

The survey collection and income/policy years are distinct and bound to the source audit in the data section.

7. Is priced consumption observed expenditure?

No. It is a simulated disposable-resource output under the stated full-year job and policy assumptions.

8. Are couples independent singles?

No. They choose joint jobs under a shared non-linear household budget.

9. What does the missing leisure interaction mean?

Its coefficient is maintained at zero, not estimated to demonstrate independent choices.

10. Where do children enter?

Female leisure weights in both types, and separate policy/needs pathways; the counts are not interchangeable.

11. Is a child coefficient a percentage?

No. It adds to the leisure weight.

12. Is a leisure weight willingness to pay?

No. A marginal rate of substitution also uses consumption and leisure levels, curvatures and units.

13. Is an hours density height a mass?

No. Its integral over the interval is mass; the narrow full-time band is not an atom.

14. Does the access intercept shift every working comparison?

No. It cancels between working jobs and shifts work against non-work.

15. What distinguishes g, p and q?

Structural opportunity intensity, utility-weighted choice density and the analyst’s numerical proposal, respectively.

16. Are simulated jobs a recovered menu?

No. They are numerical alternatives representing integrals or sampled likelihood calculations.

17. Why correct the observed row?

Under the independent conditional sampling law its proposal density appears in the same candidate correction as every other row.

18. Are historical wage draws independent?

No. Their scrambled Halton dependence invalidates the simple iid conditional-sampling derivation for that historical frame.

19. What does household-robust inference allow?

Dependence within a household’s score, conditional on the model and shared generated inputs, with independent households.

20. What does an integration band measure?

Finite numerical integration uncertainty at fixed parameters, not parameter sampling uncertainty.

21. Is a reference range a confidence interval?

No. It records normative-reference sensitivity.

22. What exactly is equivalent income?

A flat monthly disposable-consumption amount at every alternative in the stated reference opportunity distribution.

23. What did the identity check establish?

The factorized closed form reproduces the executed inversion at historical parameters for both types; it did not re-estimate the model.

24. What is special about log consumption?

Equivalent income becomes a consumption average weighted by non-consumption utility and opportunities, not by choice probabilities.

25. Must wider opportunities raise W?

No. They change attained value and the reference map; added low-consumption weight can lower the implemented average.

26. Do opportunities matter for actual non-workers?

Yes. Their ex-ante evaluation includes working and non-working alternatives.

27. Why adjust for household needs?

A household amount is not automatically comparable across rosters; the declared scale changes with composition when that pathway is equalized.

28. Is the broad environment share the opportunity share?

No. The latter is access plus wage opportunities; the former also contains resources and needs.

29. Is Shapley the one-factor reduction?

No. It averages marginal equalization effects across the permitted orders, allocating interactions.

30. Must shares sum to one?

Only if the grand-coalition residual is zero; otherwise they sum to the reducible difference divided by baseline inequality.

31. Why not report old nested percentages?

Their resource/needs classification and pricing pathways are stale, so corrected attribution is not established.

32. What does the common-opportunity benchmark identify?

A structural model comparison after re-estimation, not a causal effect or a licensed nested likelihood-ratio test.

33. Do public wage tables identify preferences?

No. They benchmark distributions and support choices under different coverage.

34. Does singles device parity establish couples support?

No. Each specification and backend must be evaluated on its own supported path.
